crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practice of packaging an analysis so that another person, or the same person months later, can rerun it and get the same result.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of putting a question to a dataset in ordinary words and getting back a computed answer, rather than writing SQL or a script by hand.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the practice of running heavy analytical workloads, such as model training, simulation, and statistical estimation, against datasets that an organisation holds under its own control rather than against public or scraped sources.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of language models and code assistants to draft, refactor, and explain analysis scripts in languages such as R, Python, and Stata.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking that a planned analysis can actually answer the question it claims to answer, using simulated or pilot data rather than the real dataset.

sections.body: Quantitative analysis with AI is the practice of using models to write, check and run the code that turns raw measurements into results. In practice this means assistants that draft Python or R for cleaning, modelling and plotting, notebooks that record every step so a run can be repeated, and natural language interfaces that translate a plain question into a query over a table. It also covers simulation work, where a study design is stress tested on synthetic data before anyone recruits a participant or pays for a sample. The aim is not to replace statistical judgement but to remove the mechanical friction of writing and re-running analysis code.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The parts that work are the routine ones. Code generation for standard transforms, regression, resampling and plotting is reliable enough to save real time, and notebook tooling for versioning and environment capture is mature. What is not solved is correctness. A model can produce code that runs without error and still answers the wrong question, mishandles missing data, or leaks information across a train and test split. Reproducibility remains fragile because environments drift, seeds are omitted and dependencies change under a project. Plain language querying is useful for exploration but weak on ambiguity, since a vague question yields a confident and wrong table. Large scale compute on institutional data adds governance, access and cost constraints that no model resolves. The honest limit is that AI accelerates the writing of analysis while offering little guarantee about its validity.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the arc of a study from setup to execution. Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines is the foundation, covering how to structure a project so results can be regenerated, and it is the page to read first if your work is not currently repeatable. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language covers the exploratory layer, where a researcher interrogates a dataset conversationally before committing to a formal model. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection sits earlier in the timeline than its position suggests, because it is about simulating an analysis plan to check that the design can actually detect what it hopes to detect. Writing Statistical Code with AI is the practical core, dealing with generated code, review and testing. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data is the infrastructure page, for work that outgrows a laptop and must run inside an institution's own systems and rules. Read together they form a sequence, and each assumes the ones before it.
